weeks.title: The Human Problem: Living Centered on Self
weeks.theme: The root of all our problems is leaving God and centering life on ourselves—what the Bible calls “sin.”
group: When you hear the word “sin,” what is your first reaction?
Where do you see yourself “turning to your own way” and being your own master?
Why is it so hard for people to become good on their own?
weeks.guide: When talking about sin, seekers easily feel accused: “I haven’t killed anyone.” Share your own sin and brokenness first, then explain that in the Bible sin isn’t only breaking laws—it is “centering life on myself and leaving God.” Use images like “heading the wrong direction” or “missing the target.” Don’t condemn; look in the mirror together. And be sure they know: the diagnosis is for healing, and the good news is coming.
weeks.meet: This week, talk with the person walking with you about one question: “For most of my life, who has been in charge?” Share honestly—no need to defend yourself.
weeks.keyText: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

lessons.title: The Root of Every Problem
text: The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
lessons.hear:
The news is full of war, fraud, domestic violence and corruption every day; homes are full of quarrels, silent treatment and hurt. Technology keeps advancing, yet the human heart doesn’t seem to improve. Where is the root of the problem? The Bible gives the answer at the very beginning.

After God created people and gave them every good thing, he set only one boundary: don’t eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The serpent tempted them: “You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:4-5). The heart of the temptation was: “You will be like God.” People were no longer content to be human; they wanted to decide for themselves what is good and evil, to be their own master, to take God’s place.

This is the root of humanity’s fall: centering life on self, insisting on being in charge. It shows itself as pride—leaving our place as humans and grabbing God’s authority. From that day, the relationship between people and God was broken, and so were relationships between people: Adam began to shift blame, and Cain killed his brother. All the world’s problems today, traced to their root, are fruit from this heart that says, “I want to be in charge.”
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our place and grabbing authority, wanting to replace God. The self-centered life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of our problems. Seeing this root isn’t meant to make us blame ourselves, but to help us find the real cure.
think: Do you agree that the human problem lies in the heart? Why?
What does the temptation “you will be like God” look like in your life today?
What was the last thing you insisted on deciding by yourself? How did it turn out?
lessons.speak: God, I’m beginning to see that I often want to be in charge, as if I knew better than you what is good. I admit this is the root of my problems. Help me see it clearly, and show me the way out. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when something makes you angry or anxious, ask yourself: “Who wants to be in charge right now?”
lessons.quick: Our problem isn’t only doing wrong—it’s wanting to replace God.

lessons.title: Everyone Has Turned to His Own Way
text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
lessons.hear:
Sheep have a tendency: they wander off easily. With heads down, they nibble grass, and nibble, and wander away from the flock. When they finally look up, they have no idea where they are. A sheep isn’t trying to rebel; it just follows its appetite. The Bible uses sheep to describe us: “All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way” (Isaiah 53:6).

“Everyone has turned to his own way” says it vividly. People go different ways: some the way of indulgence, some the way of self-righteousness; some chase money, some chase fame; some are very bad, some are very “good”—but what they share is walking their own way, not God’s way. One of the Bible’s words for “sin” has the sense of “missing the mark.” It isn’t only the arrow that hits the neighbor’s target that misses; any arrow that misses the center has missed.

So sin isn’t only breaking the law; it is the direction of life going off course—what should be centered on God is centered on self. That’s why even “good people” need God. A person may be very moral yet never need God, thank God or care about God—that is still walking one’s own way. The good news is in the second half of the same verse: “and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” God has already prepared a way out.
lessons.light: Sin isn’t only behavior but direction; not only doing wrong, but centering life on self. The self-centered life is “everyone turning to his own way.” Seeing that I am a lost sheep is the first step back to the Shepherd.
think: Which kind of “own way” do you think you tend to walk?
Do you agree that “good people need God too”? Where do you struggle with that?
What hope does the second half of the verse give you?
lessons.speak: God, I am a lost sheep too, often following my own desires and ideas with my head down, wandering farther and farther from you. Thank you for not giving up on looking for me. Please bring me back to your way. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write down a time in your life when you drifted farther and farther away, and think about what pulled you off course.
lessons.quick: Sin is missing the mark: leaving God and walking our own way.

lessons.title: What Comes from the Heart
text: He said, “That which proceeds out of the man, that defiles the man.
For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts,
covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness.
All these evil things come from within and defile the man.”
lessons.hear:
Some say, “I haven’t done anything bad, so I’m not a sinner.” Jesus moved the focus from outward behavior to the heart within: “That which proceeds out of the man, that defiles the man. For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness” (Mark 7:20-22).

That list is very honest. We may not have stolen or murdered, but what about envy? Pride? Evil thoughts in our minds? Jesus says all of these come from the heart—some grow into actions, some stay hidden inside. It’s like a tree: when the fruit is bad, the problem is in the roots. Pick off the bad fruit, and next year it grows back.

This also explains why “making a resolution” can’t change a person. We can control our temper for a while but can’t control the resentment inside; we can behave well in front of others but can’t make our hearts clean. People need more than better behavior; they need a new heart. And the Bible promises that this is exactly what God wants to do.
lessons.light: Everything we do flows from the heart. If the problem is in the heart, the cure must reach the heart. Outward change depends on ourselves; inward change depends on the Holy Spirit. Change starts with me, and my change starts with my heart.
think: Which items on Jesus’ list have you seen in your own heart?
Have you ever tried to break a bad habit by sheer resolve? What happened?
Do you think it’s possible to receive “a new heart”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you see through my heart. I admit there is envy, pride and evil thought in me that I can’t wash away. Please don’t only change my behavior—give me a new heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Observe your heart once today: when a negative emotion rises, write down its name (envy, discontent, pride). Don’t defend it—just acknowledge it.
lessons.quick: Bad fruit comes from bad roots; we need a new heart.

lessons.title: I Can’t Save Myself
text: For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.
For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.
What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?
lessons.hear:
Have you ever made a New Year’s resolution—to exercise, to spend less time on your phone, to be gentler with family—only to give up within a month? Then you blame your lack of willpower. It isn’t just you. Even the apostle Paul, who wrote much of the New Testament, admitted: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice” (Romans 7:18-19).

This is the common human dilemma: knowing is one thing, doing is another. We are like someone in quicksand—the more we struggle, the deeper we sink; or like someone trying to lift himself up by his own hair. Finally Paul cried out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

That cry is important, because it is a turning point. As long as we think “I can do it myself,” we won’t call for help. When we admit “I can’t save myself,” we start to ask “Who can save me?” Paul immediately gives the answer: through Jesus Christ our Lord. Admitting our helplessness isn’t failure; it is the beginning of being saved.
lessons.light: Pride says, “I can do it on my own.” Humility says, “I need to be rescued.” Humility is the key to revival; God gives grace to the humble. Admitting our inability is the starting point for experiencing God’s power.
think: What is one thing you resolved to do well but couldn’t carry out?
Paul cried, “What a wretched man I am!” When have you felt that way?
Is it hard for you to admit “I can’t save myself”? Why?
lessons.speak: God, I’ve tried to become good on my own, and I can’t. I know what is right, yet I often can’t do it. I admit that I can’t save myself. Who can save me? If Jesus really can, please let me know him. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Honestly write down one thing you have long wanted to change but haven’t been able to. No excuses—just write: “In this, I need help.”
lessons.quick: Admitting “I can’t save myself” is where salvation begins.

lessons.title: The Wages of Sin, the Gift of God
text: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
lessons.hear:
This week has been like a doctor’s visit, and we received an honest diagnosis: people have left God and centered life on themselves; our hearts are stained in ways we can’t wash away; we can’t save ourselves. The last line of the report reads: “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). “Wages” are what we earn by our work. Leaving the source of life results in death—not only physical death, but eternal separation from God.

But the verse isn’t finished: “but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Notice the two contrasts: “wages” versus “gift,” and “death” versus “eternal life.” Wages are earned; a gift is freely given. Death is what we deserve; eternal life is what God wants to give. It’s like someone drowning in debt he can never repay, when suddenly someone pays it all off—and gives him a new home besides.

Who is willing to pay this price? Why? How? That is the Jesus we will meet in the coming weeks. Tonight, you can go to sleep holding these two words: what I have earned are “wages”; what God wants to give is a “gift.”
lessons.light: First we see our own problem; then we can see God’s grace. The more clearly we see how serious sin is, the more precious grace becomes. The gospel isn’t advice on how to be better; it is a gift God gives freely.
think: What is the difference between “wages” and a “gift”?
What do you think you deserve? What does God want to give you?
Why would someone refuse a free gift?
lessons.speak: God, now I understand that the wages of sin is death—that’s what I deserve. But you say you want to freely give me eternal life. That’s so good I hardly dare believe it. Help me understand this gift, and Jesus who gives it. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Memorize Romans 6:23. Try explaining the difference between “wages” and “gift” to someone in your own words.
lessons.quick: I deserve death; God freely offers eternal life.

weeks.title: Who Is Jesus?
weeks.theme: Jesus is God who became human, the friend of sinners, and the only way to the Father.
group: What was your impression of Jesus before?
Which story about Jesus this week impressed you most?
If Jesus asked you, “Who do you say that I am?” how would you answer?
weeks.guide: This week’s goal is to help the seeker “meet Jesus,” not just “understand Christianity.” Read a Gospel story together (for example, Zacchaeus) and ask, “What kind of person do you think Jesus is?” Many are moved by Jesus’ love for the marginalized. If they ask, “Why is Jesus the only way?”, affirm that it’s a good question, then gently share: this isn’t Christian arrogance—Jesus himself said it; if he is God, this statement is love pointing the way.
weeks.meet: This week, read the story of Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1-10) with the person walking with you and talk about it: if Jesus came to your home for dinner, what would he see?
weeks.keyText: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.

lessons.title: The Word Became Flesh
text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The same was in the beginning with God.
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
lessons.hear:
If you wanted a colony of ants to know that you love them, how would you do it? They can’t understand your words, and if you come close they panic. Perhaps the only way would be to become an ant yourself and live with them in a way they understand. The illustration isn’t perfect, but it helps us grasp the most amazing meaning of Christmas.

John’s Gospel begins: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). “Word” is how God expresses himself. Then John writes a sentence that shook history: “The Word became flesh and lived among us… full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The God who created the universe became a human being—born in a manger, raised in a carpenter’s home, knowing hunger, tiredness, tears and being misunderstood.

This is Jesus. He is not merely a great teacher, prophet or religious founder; the Bible says he is God who became human. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus. His gentleness is God’s gentleness, his tears are God’s tears, and his welcome of sinners is God’s welcome of you.
lessons.light: God didn’t shout from far away; he stepped into our world himself. Jesus is my example: he laid aside heaven’s glory and humbled himself to become human. This is the highest display of selflessness—giving up everything for love.
think: Did you think of Jesus as God, a man, or a great person?
How does the idea “God became human” make you feel?
If God is willing to step into your situation, what would you most want him to see?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that, so I could know God, you laid aside your glory, became human and lived among us. So God is not far away—you are willing to come into my life. Please let me know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read John 1:1-14 and highlight the sentence you find most beautiful. Make it into a verse card for yourself.
lessons.quick: To see what God is like, look at Jesus.

lessons.title: What He Did
text: Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk’?
But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” —he said to the paralytic—
“I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.”
He arose, and immediately took up the mat and went out in front of them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”
lessons.hear:
Four friends carried a paralyzed man to Jesus, but the house was so packed they couldn’t get in. So they climbed onto the roof, opened a hole in it, and lowered their friend, mat and all, right in front of Jesus. Seeing their faith, the first thing Jesus said to the paralyzed man was: “Your sins are forgiven.”

The religious leaders there grumbled in their hearts: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” They were right—only God can forgive sins. Jesus knew their thoughts and said: “Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk’?” (Mark 2:9). Then he said to the man, “I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.” He arose, and immediately took up the mat and went out in front of them all (Mark 2:11-12).

Jesus used a visible miracle to prove an invisible fact: he has authority to forgive sins. He healed the sick, calmed storms and raised the dead—not as magic shows, but as signs pointing to who he is. He cares not only about people’s bodies but about their deepest need: to be reconciled to God.
lessons.light: People matter more than things: four friends tore open a roof to bring their friend to Jesus. That is what spiritual parents do. And what Jesus cares about most isn’t just solving problems, but restoring people’s relationship with God.
think: Why do you think those four friends went to such lengths?
Why do you think Jesus said “Your sins are forgiven” before healing his body?
Is there someone in your life willing to “carry you to Jesus”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you have power to heal, and authority to forgive sins. There are paralyzed places in my life too, and sins that need forgiving. I bring myself to you—please heal me and forgive me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Thank God for the person walking with you (or a friend who cares for you), and send them a thank-you message.
lessons.quick: Jesus doesn’t only heal bodies—he has authority to forgive sins.

lessons.title: What He Said
text: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”
lessons.hear:
Many great teachers in history have said, “I teach you a way” or “I have discovered the truth.” But Jesus spoke very differently. He didn’t just point to the light; he said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). He also said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me” (John 14:6).

If an ordinary person said such things, he would be either mad or a fraud. Someone who claims to be the truth and the way to God can’t be “just a good teacher.” The British writer C. S. Lewis observed that when it comes to Jesus we have only three options: he was a liar, a lunatic, or he really was who he said he was—the Lord.

Jesus’ words aren’t arrogant boasting. If he truly is God, then “I am the light of the world” is the best news in the dark of night. Like someone lost in the mountains who hears a guide say, “Follow me, I am the way”—that isn’t arrogance; it’s rescue. Today Jesus invites you too: follow me, and you will not walk in darkness.
lessons.light: The focus is Jesus: he isn’t only the one who points the way; he is the way. Following Jesus isn’t following a set of rules; it is following a person. Jesus is my example and my way.
think: Do you agree that Jesus can’t be “just a good teacher”? Why?
What dark places in your life need light?
What might the invitation “follow me” mean for you?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you say you are the light of the world. I admit my life has darkness and confusion. If you truly are the light and the way, I want to follow you and no longer walk in darkness. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, after turning off the lights, switch on a small lamp. Notice how darkness retreats when light comes. Bring one “dark” thing that troubles you to Jesus in one sentence.
lessons.quick: Jesus doesn’t just point the way—he is the way.

lessons.title: Friend of Sinners
text: When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”
lessons.hear:
Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector in Jericho. He collected taxes for the Roman government and often took extra for himself. He was rich, but the whole town despised him. One day he heard Jesus was passing through. Being short, he couldn’t see over the crowd, so he climbed a sycamore tree.

When Jesus reached the spot, he looked up and called him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). The townspeople muttered, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” But something wonderful happened in Zacchaeus’ house that day. Zacchaeus stood up and said: “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much” (Luke 19:8). No one forced him; Jesus’ acceptance melted his heart.

Jesus said, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). Jesus was called “a friend of sinners.” He didn’t approve of sin, but he loved sinners; he didn’t wait for people to change before coming—when he came, people changed. Maybe you feel like Zacchaeus, looked down on and watching from the tree. Today Jesus is calling your name too.
lessons.light: Zacchaeus wasn’t scolded into changing—he was loved into changing. Humility brings out humility: Jesus humbled himself to enter a sinner’s home, and Zacchaeus let go of his greed. God’s grace comes first; a changed life follows.
think: Why do you think Zacchaeus was willing to change?
Jesus called Zacchaeus by name. What does that mean to you?
Is there a “sycamore tree” place in your heart—wanting to get close to Jesus, but afraid to be seen?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for being the friend of sinners. There are parts of me I don’t want anyone to see, but you see them—and still call my name. I want to come down. Please come into my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Think: is there anything in your life you need to make right or apologize for? Write it down and ask God for courage.
lessons.quick: Jesus didn’t wait for people to change—when he came, they changed.

lessons.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
text: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
lessons.hear:
One day Jesus asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” They answered: some say John the Baptist, some Elijah, some one of the prophets. These were all high opinions. Then Jesus turned the question to them: “But who do you say that I am?” (Matthew 16:15).

Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). “Christ” means “the Anointed One,” the Savior. Peter didn’t say “You are a good teacher,” but “You are the Savior God promised would come.” Jesus said this wasn’t something people had told him; the Father had revealed it to him.

“Who do others say Jesus is?” is a question of knowledge. “Who do you say Jesus is?” is a question of life. You can know many things about Jesus without ever answering this question. This week we have seen that Jesus is God who became human, the Lord with authority to forgive, the light of the world, and the friend of sinners. Now Jesus gently asks you: “Who do you say that I am?” You don’t need a complete answer today, but please face the question honestly.
lessons.light: The turning point of faith is moving from “others say” to “I say.” In the eight steps of changing our mindset, after “Information” comes “Revelation”—asking God himself to show you who Jesus is. Head knowledge needs heart revelation.
think: Among your friends and family, who do people say Jesus is?
After this week, how would you yourself answer “Who is Jesus?”
What still stops you from believing that Jesus is the Christ?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you ask me, “Who do you say that I am?” I want to answer you honestly, but I still need you to reveal yourself to me. Father, let me see who Jesus is, so that my answer isn’t just what others say, but what I say. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write one sentence: “Right now, I believe Jesus is…” Come back to it in a few weeks and see whether your answer has changed.
lessons.quick: Better than what others say about Jesus is what I say about him.

weeks.title: The Cross: Where Love and Justice Meet
weeks.theme: On the cross, God’s justice judged sin, and God’s love saved sinners.
group: When you used to see a cross, what did you think of?
What does “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” mean to you?
What do the two criminals beside the cross teach you?
weeks.guide: The cross is the heart of the gospel. This week, a simple picture can help (for example, the “Bridge”: a canyon of sin between people and God, with the cross of Jesus as the bridge). Ask often, “Why do you think Jesus had to die?” without rushing to give the textbook answer. If the seeker is moved and tears up, don’t rush ahead; give them quiet time and ask, “Is there anything you want to say to God?”
weeks.meet: This week, read the account of the crucifixion in Luke 23 with the person walking with you, and quietly give thanks for Jesus’ suffering.
weeks.keyText: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

lessons.title: Why Did He Have to Die?
text: Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
lessons.hear:
If God is love, why not simply forgive everyone? Why the cross? Imagine a judge whose son has committed a serious crime and is brought before his court. If the judge declares him innocent because he loves him, he is not a just judge. If he sentences him strictly, his heart breaks for his son. In the end, the judge pronounces the lawful sentence, then takes off his robe, steps down, and pays the entire penalty for his son.

That is the cross. God is just—sin must be judged. God is love—he doesn’t want people to perish. On the cross, God himself bore the judgment for sin. Isaiah said seven hundred years earlier: “Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering… But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:4-5).

Jesus wasn’t an unfortunate martyr; he was a willing substitute. He carried not his own sins but ours; he received not what he deserved but what we deserved. This is the cross: justice and mercy meet here.
lessons.light: On the cross Jesus gave himself completely—the ultimate selfless love. God’s justice was not discounted; God’s love held nothing back. We can have peace because he bore the punishment.
think: Which side of the cross does the judge illustration help you understand?
“He was pierced for our transgressions”—can you put yourself in that “our”?
Have God’s love and God’s justice ever seemed to conflict in your mind?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, so the suffering you endured on the cross was for me. You carried my sin and my pain so that I could have peace. I don’t know how to repay such love; all I can say is: thank you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Find a cross (a necklace, a church, a picture). Look at it quietly for one minute and say to Jesus, “This was for me.”
lessons.quick: On the cross, justice judged sin and mercy saved sinners.

lessons.title: While We Were Yet Sinners
text: For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
lessons.hear:
Very few people in this world are willing to die for someone else. Paul says: “For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die” (Romans 5:7). For a good person or a benefactor, maybe someone would give their life. But who would die for an enemy, for someone who betrayed them?

The Bible continues: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Notice the timing: not after we became good, not after we repented, but “while we were yet sinners.” While we still turned our backs on God, ignored him, even mocked him, Jesus had already gone to the cross for us.

This shows that God’s love is not a deal. Many people spend their whole lives trying to “deserve love”: good grades, a good income, being a good person. But God’s love isn’t a reward; it’s a gift. Not because you are good enough, but because he is love. You don’t have to clean yourself up before coming to God. At your worst, he already loved you.
lessons.light: God’s love doesn’t look at our performance. When we realize we were loved when we least deserved it, pride loses its footing and inferiority loses its grip. That is grace: undeserved, yet received.
think: Have you ever worked hard to “deserve” love?
How is being loved “while we were yet sinners” different from your previous understanding of love?
If God loved you at your worst, what do you still need to fear?
lessons.speak: God, I often feel I must be good enough to be loved. But you say that while I was still a sinner, Jesus died for me. Thank you for loving me like this. I’m willing to stop proving myself and receive your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Copy Romans 5:8 and write your name beside “us.”
lessons.quick: God didn’t wait for me to get better—he loved me at my worst.

lessons.title: Father, Forgive Them
text: When they came to the place that is called “The Skull”, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on the right and the other on the left.
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots.
lessons.hear:
Crucifixion was the cruelest punishment of the Roman Empire. Nails pierced the hands and feet; the victim hung on the wood, struggling to breathe, often suffering for hours before dying. If we were treated like that, what came out of our mouths might be curses, hatred or cries for help.

But one of the first things Jesus said on the cross was: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He prayed for the soldiers nailing him, and pleaded for those mocking him. This isn’t weakness; it is a love beyond human imagination. In his greatest pain, his heart was still on others.

“Them” includes us. Our pride, selfishness and indifference were part of what nailed Jesus to the cross. Yet Jesus’ prayer is for us too: “Father, forgive them.” This is the gospel: the most serious sin meets the deepest forgiveness. If Jesus could forgive those who crucified him, he can forgive anything you have done.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride; hatred breeds hatred. But humility brings out humility, and forgiveness ends hatred. On the cross Jesus lived out selfless love: praying for his enemies. This is the pattern we learn after being forgiven.
think: What kind of heart does it take to pray for your enemies in such pain?
Is there something you feel “can never be forgiven”?
Is there someone in your life who is very hard to forgive?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the cross you prayed for those who crucified you—and for me. Many things in me need forgiveness; please forgive me. I also bring to you someone I find hard to forgive. Please give me a forgiving heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write down the thing you most want to be forgiven for, and the name of someone you need to forgive. Bring this paper before God, then tear it up.
lessons.quick: The deepest sin meets an even deeper forgiveness.

lessons.title: Today You Will Be with Me in Paradise
text: One of the criminals who was hanged insulted him, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!”
But the other answered, and rebuking him said, “Don’t you even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation?
And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward for our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong.”
He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.”
Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
lessons.hear:
Two criminals were crucified with Jesus. One joined in the mocking: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!” But the other rebuked him: “We indeed justly, for we receive the due reward for our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong.” Then he said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

Jesus answered, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). This criminal had no chance to be baptized, read the Bible or do good works to make up for his past. He did only three things: admitted his own sin, acknowledged Jesus’ innocence, and asked Jesus for help. And he was saved.

Both criminals were equally close to Jesus, yet their endings were completely different. The difference wasn’t whose sins were fewer, but who was willing to turn humbly to Jesus. This gives enormous hope to everyone who thinks “it’s too late” or “I’m too bad”: as long as you have breath, it is never too late to call on Jesus.
lessons.light: One stayed proud to the end; one turned humbly to Jesus. Salvation doesn’t depend on our merit but on returning to our place: admitting I am a sinner and acknowledging he is the Savior. This is humility overcoming pride.
think: Which of the two criminals do you identify with more?
This man was saved with a single sentence. How does that make you feel?
Is there someone near you who thinks, “I’m too bad—God wouldn’t want me”?
lessons.speak: Jesus, like that criminal, I receive what I deserve, but you have done nothing wrong. I want to say to you too: Lord, remember me! Thank you for promising that you turn no one away who calls on you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Think of a family member or friend who seems “far from God,” and pray one sentence for them today: “Lord, remember them too.”
lessons.quick: Turning to Jesus is never too late.

lessons.title: It Is Finished!
text: After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty!”
Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished!” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
lessons.hear:
One of the last things Jesus said on the cross was: “It is finished!” (John 19:30). In the original language this is a single word. In business documents of that time, it meant “paid in full.” Archaeologists have found ancient receipts stamped with this very word.

Jesus wasn’t saying, “I’m done for,” but “It is finished”—the work of salvation is complete, the debt of sin paid in full. He didn’t leave a portion for us to make up, or say, “The rest is up to your effort.” It’s like a bill stamped “PAID”: you don’t have to pay another cent, and you can’t.

Many religions tell people: work hard at spiritual practice and good deeds, and you may be saved. But the gospel tells us: Jesus has paid in full. We don’t work in order to be saved; we live gratefully because we are saved. This week we stood before the cross and saw God’s justice and mercy. Next week we will see the most astonishing event after the cross: Jesus rose from the dead.
lessons.light: Everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus—all grace. Wanting to add our own merit is a sign of the self-centered life; accepting “It is finished” means laying ourselves down and giving all the glory to Jesus.
think: What is the difference between “It is finished” and “I’m finished”?
How much did you think salvation depended on your own effort?
If the debt of sin is paid in full, how do you most want to respond?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for saying, “It is finished.” You have paid my debt of sin in full; I don’t have to repay it myself. I accept the salvation you have completed, and I want to live with a grateful heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: On a piece of paper write “My debt of sin,” then write a large “PAID IN FULL” across it and put it where you can see it.
lessons.quick: “It is finished”—Jesus has paid it all.

weeks.title: Resurrection: Death Is Not the End
weeks.theme: Jesus rose from the dead, proving he is the Son of God and giving us eternal hope.
group: How do you think about what happens after death?
Which evidence for the resurrection impressed you most?
If Jesus really rose, how would that change your today?
weeks.guide: The resurrection is central to faith and one of seekers’ biggest questions. Share clues such as the witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15, the disciples’ transformation and the empty tomb—and also your own “resurrection life” since believing: what old thing died and what new thing came alive. Be especially gentle this week with seekers who have recently lost loved ones; let them know the hope of resurrection is real comfort. At the end of the week you might ask, “Are you ready to receive Jesus, or do you still have questions?” No pressure—just an invitation.
weeks.meet: This week, talk with the person walking with you: if you knew death was not the end, how would you want to live the days ahead?
weeks.keyText: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.

lessons.title: The Empty Tomb
text: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb.
They entered in, and didn’t find the Lord Jesus’ body.
While they were greatly perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling clothing.
Becoming terrified, they bowed their faces down to the earth. The men said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?
He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee,
lessons.hear:
After Jesus was crucified and buried, the disciples hid, afraid and hopeless. Early on the third day, some women brought spices to the tomb to anoint his body. On the way they worried: who will roll away the huge stone from the entrance for us?

When they arrived, the stone had already been rolled away, and the tomb was empty. Two men in dazzling clothing said to them: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He isn’t here, but is risen” (Luke 24:5-6). Terrified, they ran to tell the disciples, who at first thought they were talking nonsense.

The empty tomb is a historical fact that is hard to explain away. If Jesus’ body were still there, his opponents only had to produce it, and Christianity would have ended. No one could. Some said the disciples stole the body, but the tomb was guarded by Roman soldiers and sealed; and the disciples later preached the resurrection even when it cost them their lives—no one dies for a lie he made up. Jesus rose from the dead. This is the foundation of the Christian faith.
lessons.light: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” We too often look for life among dead things: past achievements, old relationships, possessions that decay. The focus is the living Jesus; he is the source of life.
think: The women worried about the stone all the way there, and it had already been rolled away. What does that remind you of?
What do you think is the most reasonable explanation of the empty tomb?
Where in your life might you be “seeking the living among the dead”?
lessons.speak: Risen Lord Jesus, if you really rose from the dead, then you are alive today, and you can hear me. Please let me meet you, the living one. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read Luke 24:1-12. Imagine you are one of the women going to the tomb that morning, and write down how you would feel seeing it empty.
lessons.quick: He isn’t in the tomb—he is risen.

lessons.title: More Than Five Hundred Witnesses
text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep.
Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles,
and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
lessons.hear:
About twenty-some years after Jesus’ resurrection, Paul wrote to the church in Corinth with a list of witnesses: “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:3-6).

“Most of whom remain until now” is a bold statement. It’s as if Paul were saying: “If you don’t believe it, go and ask them.” If the resurrection were invented, writing this would be asking for trouble. And Jesus didn’t appear to just one or two people, but at different times and places to different people—once to more than five hundred at the same time.

Even more powerful evidence is the change in the disciples. When Jesus was arrested they scattered; Peter denied him three times. Yet weeks later the same group was publicly proclaiming in Jerusalem that Jesus had risen, unafraid of beatings and prison, and most eventually died as martyrs. What turned a group of frightened men into bold witnesses? They said: we saw him alive with our own eyes.
lessons.light: The resurrection isn’t only a doctrine; it is power that changes lives. Fearful Peter became a bold apostle—changing the mindset changes the life, and changing the life changes the way we live. The same power can change you today.
think: How does “most of whom remain until now” strike you?
How does the disciples’ transformation help you believe in the resurrection?
Have you seen anyone’s life changed by believing in Jesus?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, those fearful disciples became brave because they saw you risen. I have many weaknesses and fears too. Let your resurrection power change me as well. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Ask the person walking with you (or a Christian friend): “How has your life changed since believing in Jesus?” Listen carefully to their story.
lessons.quick: Frightened people became bold because they saw him alive.

lessons.title: Thomas’ Doubt
text: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days, again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”
lessons.hear:
When Jesus first appeared to the disciples after rising, Thomas happened to be absent. The others told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But Thomas said, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25). He was a practical man who wanted evidence.

Eight days later Jesus came again, and this time Thomas was there. Jesus didn’t rebuke him; he walked straight to him and said: “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing” (John 20:27). Thomas immediately made the highest confession in all the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

Then Jesus said, “Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.” That sentence is for us. We weren’t in that room, but we have the testimony of those who were. God isn’t afraid of your doubts; he is willing to answer sincere questions himself. Come with your questions. Like Thomas, one day you may also say: “My Lord and my God!”
lessons.light: Jesus respects honest questions and walks toward the doubter. Doubt isn’t sin; proudly rejecting evidence is the real obstacle. Humble doubt leads people toward faith, as it did for Thomas.
think: Like Thomas, do you need evidence? What do you need to see?
Jesus didn’t rebuke Thomas. What kind of Jesus do you see here?
How do you understand “Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, sometimes I’m like Thomas—I need to see before I believe. Thank you for not rebuking my doubts and for coming toward me instead. Please show yourself to me too, so that one day I can truly say, “My Lord and my God!” In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write down your current questions about Jesus’ resurrection. Look for answers in the Questions tab or ask Xiaozhi, and discuss them with the person walking with you.
lessons.quick: God isn’t afraid of doubt—he walks toward sincere questions.

lessons.title: I Am the Resurrection
text: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
lessons.hear:
Jesus’ good friend Lazarus fell ill and died. By the time Jesus arrived, he had been in the tomb four days. Lazarus’ sister Martha said in grief, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” Jesus answered with words that have changed countless lives: “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25-26).

Afterward Jesus also wept at the tomb. He knew he was about to raise Lazarus, yet he still wept over his friends’ pain. Then he called in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” And the man dead four days came out, bound hand and foot with grave clothes.

Death is life’s biggest problem; every achievement, relationship and fortune is reset to zero before it. But Jesus says he is the resurrection and the life. For those who believe in him, death isn’t the end but a door to eternity. This isn’t only future hope; it’s strength for today: when you know the ending is good, you have courage to face present trouble. Today Jesus asks you too: “Do you believe this?”
lessons.light: Jesus wept and acted in power at the same time: he understands our pain and has conquered our death. Move from a temporary perspective to an eternal one: with eternal hope, today’s suffering takes on a different meaning.
think: Have you experienced the pain of losing family or friends?
Jesus wept at the tomb. What new understanding of him does this give you?
“Do you believe this?” How would you answer?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you say you are the resurrection and the life. I fear death, and I fear losing those I love. Thank you for understanding my tears, and even more for conquering death. I want to believe your words. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: If someone you miss has passed away, tell Jesus about your longing today. If someone near you is grieving, send them a word of care.
lessons.quick: For those who believe in Jesus, death isn’t the end—it’s a door.

lessons.title: A Living Hope
text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
to an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn’t fade away, reserved in Heaven for you,
lessons.hear:
Peter was the disciple who denied the Lord three times. After the resurrection, Jesus came looking for him and restored him, and he became a leader of the early church. Years later he wrote to believers who were suffering, and his first words were praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3).

What is a “living hope”? The world’s hope is often “hope so”: hoping tomorrow will be better, hoping the illness will pass, hoping the kids will behave—but not certain. The hope that comes from the resurrection is “know so,” because Jesus has gone ahead and opened the door of death. Peter calls it “an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn’t fade away” (1 Peter 1:4).

Stage two ends here. We have seen the human problem (centering life on self, unable to save ourselves), who Jesus is, the love of the cross, and the hope of the resurrection. That is the whole gospel. In the next stage we face the most important question: how should I respond? God has prepared the gift; now it’s our turn to decide whether to reach out and receive it.
lessons.light: With a living hope, people can stand firm in suffering. Move from an earthly to a heavenly perspective, from a temporary to an eternal one. This hope doesn’t depend on us but on Jesus’ resurrection.
think: Is your hope right now more like “hope so” or “know so”?
Looking back on stage two, which truth moved you most?
Facing the gospel, what is your biggest question or obstacle right now?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for preparing a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection. I have heard the gospel, and I want to understand more clearly how to respond to you. Please prepare my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: In five sentences, write the gospel as you understand it now: our problem, who Jesus is, the cross, the resurrection, and my response. Show it to the person walking with you.
lessons.quick: Because Jesus rose, my hope is certain.
